sections.h2: How does a house sale in Nashville work with one combined city and county government?
sections.html:
Nashville and Davidson County merged in 1963, so one Metro government handles the valuation, billing and recording steps of a sale. Belle Meade, Ridgetop and Goodlettsville are the exceptions: they levy a separate city tax. The city sits on the Cumberland River in the Nashville Basin, and the hills of the Highland Rim wrap around its western side, so sloped lots and retaining walls are part of many listings.

For July 1, 2025 the Census Bureau estimates 721,074 residents in the Nashville-Davidson balance, 4.6% above the April 2020 base. Just 52.4% of occupied units are lived in by their owners, which means plenty of sellers are landlords, heirs or people relocating for work. The table lists the Metro offices a seller is most likely to deal with.

Metro officeIts role in a saleContact detail
Register of DeedsFiles the deed and collects state recording tax300 Deaderick St, weekdays 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.
TrusteeSends tax bills and takes paymentHoward Office Building, 700 President Ronald Reagan Way, Suite 220

sections.h2: What does the Census say about homes and households in Nashville?
sections.html:
Census QuickFacts puts the typical owner-occupied home at $413,600 (2020 to 2024 figures) and median gross rent at $1,586 a month. Davidson County's balance holds 313,513 households averaging 2.13 people. Roughly four in five residents had stayed at the same address for the past year.

  • Median household income: $77,371 in 2024 dollars
  • Adults with a bachelor's degree or higher: 48.0%
  • Average commute: 24.7 minutes each way
  • Share of people in poverty: 14.1%

Treat these as citywide averages. A condo near downtown and a ranch house in Antioch can sit far apart from them, so ask for recent sales on your own street before you set a price. The figures come from Census QuickFacts.

sections.h2: Why did Nashville tax bills jump after the 2025 reappraisal?
sections.html:
Values were mailed on April 18, 2025 and the median parcel rose 45%, with council district medians running from 38% to 54%. The Assessor points out that the state first cut the old rates to revenue-neutral ones, then Metro lifted them to $2.814 per $100 assessed in the Urban Services District and $2.782 in the General Services District. That is a 26% and a 39% rise over the certified rates. A value can be appealed; the rate cannot.

Residential property is assessed at 25% of appraised value. Take the Census median of $413,600: assessed value is about $103,400, and the Trustee's method yields roughly $2,909 in the Urban Services District or $2,876 elsewhere in the county. Informal reviews for 2025 closed on May 9 and formal appeals on June 27. Both dates are behind us, so call the Assessor at 615-862-6059 to learn how a future review works.

sections.h2: What does a Nashville seller owe the Trustee at closing?
sections.html:
The October bill covers one calendar year, and it is addressed to whoever owned the parcel of record when it was printed. Your title company should split it on the closing statement. Anything unpaid stays with the parcel, so confirm the year is settled before you hand over keys.

  • Bills go out in the first week of October and the due date is the first Monday of that month.
  • The interest-free window ends the last day of February.
  • From March 1 the Trustee adds 1.5% each month.
  • Cards carry a 2.55% fee, minimum $2.00; e-checks cost $1.00.

The Trustee notes that no law requires a mailed notice, so a bill that never arrives does not erase interest. Parcels that stay delinquent can be offered at a tax sale, and the owner then has one year to redeem.

sections.h2: Which Nashville tax relief programs matter when selling?
sections.html:
Two programs help older and disabled owners: reimbursement for low-income elderly or disabled homeowners, and a freeze that locks the bill at the first qualifying year. The Comptroller's 2026 list sets Davidson County's freeze income cap at $54,900, and applicants must reach age 65 by December 31 of the tax year. A veteran with a 100% service-connected rating faces no income test, and relief covers the first $175,000 of value.

If you receive one of these breaks, tell the buyer's side early so the closing numbers reflect the actual bill. Call the Trustee at 615-862-6330 with questions about which documents prove age, residence and income.

sections.h2: What does the Davidson County Register of Deeds need from a seller?
sections.html:
The office moved to 300 Deaderick Street, and it also accepts remote filings. Tennessee charges $0.37 per $100 of price on a transfer, collected when the deed is recorded. Documents must be originals with notarized signatures. Staff cannot write a deed, and they do not report liens, since that falls to an attorney or title company.

Records are online for subscribers, and the office can tell you the date and reference number of any filing. Ask the buyer's closer to record the day you sign so the new deed shows up in the index without delay. The same office can furnish a certified copy of a deed you already hold.

sections.h2: Does a short term rental permit stay with a Nashville house?
sections.html:
It does not. Metro Codes says the permit is tied to a named person and a single address, and a change of owner cancels it, even a move from a person into a trust or LLC. A buyer who wants nightly rentals must file a new application.

  • A permit lapses 365 days after issue unless renewed.
  • The guest count tops out at twice the sleeping rooms plus four, never more than 12.
  • Renters must be 21 or older.
  • Three code violations can cost the holder the permit.

List the permit status in your offer paperwork so the buyer is not surprised. The Metro Codes operating rules spell out every condition.

sections.h2: What is the story behind Nashville's older neighborhoods?
sections.html:
Settlers built Fort Nashborough in 1779 beside the Cumberland. The town was incorporated in 1806, became the state's permanent capital in 1843, and a Metro charter joined it to the county in 1963. Nashville's public schools date to Hume School in 1855, and the unified Metro district now lists 160 schools.

Housing from many eras sits side by side. Sellers of older houses can pull the year built and living area from the Assessor's record and check them against the listing. Roof age, foundation movement and old wiring are the items buyers most often ask about, so price those in or fix them before showings.

sections.h2: What are the quickest ways to sell a Nashville house?
sections.html:
A listing reaches the most buyers but brings showings, appraisals and repair requests. A sale to a cash buyer who takes the house as-is trades some of that reach for speed, since closing waits on title work and not on a lender.

With any route, get the price in writing, confirm in the contract who pays recording tax, and let a title company prepare and record the deed. Clear liens, unpaid tax and any short term rental permit issues before the closing date.

faqs.q: Will I owe Davidson County tax if I sell in November?
faqs.a: Yes, for your share of the year. The October bill covers the whole calendar year and goes to the owner of record, so the closing statement should divide it between you and the buyer.

faqs.q: Can a Nashville owner contest the tax rate?
faqs.a: No. The Assessor says only values can be appealed. The Mayor and Metro Council set the rate, which for 2025 was $2.814 in the Urban Services District and $2.782 in the General Services District.

faqs.q: How much does the state charge to record a Nashville deed?
faqs.a: The transfer tax is $0.37 per $100 of price, and the state recording fee has a $10 minimum. The Register of Deeds has an online calculator for exact totals.

faqs.q: Can a buyer take over my short term rental permit?
faqs.a: No. Metro Codes bars assignment to another person, entity or address, and a change of ownership cancels the permit. The new owner must apply again.

faqs.q: Where can I pay Metro property tax in person?
faqs.a: At the Trustee's office, Suite 220 of the Howard Office Building, 700 President Ronald Reagan Way. Hours are weekdays 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. Mail goes to PO Box 196358, Nashville, TN 37219-6358.
